title: Philadelphia's Academy of Natural Sciences Museum Closes, Prompting Efforts to Reopen
summary:
Philadelphia's Academy of Natural Sciences Museum closed on September 30, 2026, leaving families and community leaders asking whether its public exhibits can return. The announcement came on September 1, giving visitors about a month to make a final trip.

Founded in 1812, the Academy opened to the public in 1828. It became the first place in the world to display a dinosaur skeleton in 1868. Its exhibits also included mammal dioramas, which are scenes showing animals in their habitats, live animals and changing displays.

Drexel University took financial responsibility for the Academy in 2011. It said costs rose and attendance fell after the pandemic. Drexel has faced its own financial pressures, including declining university enrollment and a budget shortfall reported in 2024.

The museum reduced hours and laid off some staff in 2025. It later canceled its 2026 summer camp. Yet attendance surged during its final weeks, and revenue was more than 20 times higher than the previous September.

Supporters held rallies and marches and gathered more than 114,000 petition signatures. Some criticized Drexel for giving little notice and not explaining what keeping the museum open would cost. Drexel said it remained committed to protecting the Academy's legacy.

Less than a week before closing, the William Penn Foundation offered a year of bridge funding: temporary money intended to allow time to find a lasting solution. Drexel said it was exploring that possibility but would need a plan for long-term financial stability before considering reopening.

The Academy's collection contains more than 19 million specimens, including plant samples gathered by Lewis and Clark. It also holds 73,000 holotypes, preserved reference samples scientists use to define and name species. Drexel says students and researchers will retain access, but access for the general public remains uncertain.

Philadelphia's city council proposed zoning changes that would make selling the building or converting it to other uses harder. It also plans public hearings to investigate the closure and possible solutions. These efforts leave the museum's future an open question.
why_it_matters: The closure limits public visits to a longstanding natural history museum. The funding offer and city proposals concern whether its exhibits can reopen while its scientific collection remains available for study.
